0.title: The Hidden Hand That Holds All Things
0.overview:
The book of Esther never mentions God. There is no prayer recorded in it, no miracle, no prophet and no voice from heaven. A Persian king throws a party, a queen is deposed, a Jewish girl wins a beauty contest, a proud official plots genocide, and a king has a sleepless night. And yet by the end, God's people have been saved, their enemy has been hanged on his own gallows, and every reader knows exactly who was at work. That is providence: God's hidden hand in ordinary events.

The providence of God is his constant care and control of all his creatures and all their actions. He did not make the world and leave it to run by itself. He sustains it every moment, works through all its events and directs everything toward his good purposes. In him we live and move and have our being (Acts 17:28).

The companion study on the Sovereignty of God shows that God rules over all things. This study looks more closely at how that rule works out in daily life: in the weather and the harvest, in the meeting of strangers and the timing of events, in hard seasons and good ones, in our decisions and plans, and in the habits of a heart that trusts God's providence.

Old believers often spoke of "reading providence," looking back over their lives to see God's hand. They also warned against reading it too quickly, as if every event were a message. Both lessons are in this study. Providence is to be trusted always, understood sometimes, and never treated as new revelation. God speaks in his word. In his providence he acts.

Six units: (1) What Providence Is; (2) Providence in the Natural World; (3) The Hidden Hand in Ordinary Lives; (4) Hard Providences; (5) Providence, Guidance and Our Choices; (6) Living by Providence.

1.title: What Providence Is
1.overview:
The word "providence" is related to "provide," and it carries the idea of God seeing ahead and caring for what he has made. When Abraham was asked by Isaac where the lamb for the sacrifice was, he answered, God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son (Gen 22:8). Afterward he named the place The LORD will provide (Gen 22:14). Providence is God seeing to it.

Christians have usually described providence in three parts.

Preservation. God keeps everything in existence. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them; and you preserve all of them (Neh 9:6). Christ holds all things together (Col 1:17). Nothing continues by its own power.

Concurrence. God works in and through the actions of his creatures. When rain falls, wind blows or a farmer harvests, God is at work, not instead of these causes but through them. When people make real choices, God is at work in and through them too, without making them puppets and without sharing in their sin.

Government. God directs all things to their appointed end. History is not a random series of events but a story with an author, moving toward the day when Christ will be all in all.

Providence is therefore both universal and particular. It covers galaxies and sparrows, empires and households. And it is personal. The God of providence is not a cosmic machine but a Father. Jesus did not say "nature feeds the birds" but your heavenly Father feeds them (Matt 6:26).
1.theology:
Providence is not deism: Deism pictures God as a watchmaker who made the world, wound it up and walked away. Scripture's God is never absent. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us (Acts 17:27).

Providence is not chance: Chance is not a power. When Scripture says a man drew his bow at random (1 Kgs 22:34), it means at random from the archer's point of view. From God's point of view, that arrow was the fulfilment of a prophecy (1 Kgs 22:17, 37-38).

Providence uses means: God ordinarily works through means: food, medicine, work, wise counsel and prayer. Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Tim 5:23). Trusting providence never means neglecting the means God has given.

Providence serves redemption: All of God's providence finally serves his purpose in Christ. The history of the world is the stage on which God gathers his people and glorifies his Son. Every providence in a believer's life is part of that larger story.
1.examples:
Then: King Ahab disguised himself in battle to escape the prophet's warning that he would die. But a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the scale armor and the breastplate (1 Kgs 22:34). An unknown soldier, aiming at no one in particular, fulfilled the word of God. Disguises do not work on providence.

Then: During a drought, God fed Elijah by ravens at a brook, then by a widow whose flour and oil did not run out (1 Kgs 17:4-16). He used birds, water and a poor woman's kitchen. Providence is often ordinary means made extraordinary in their timing.

Now: A family's car breaks down on a long journey. They are frustrated and late. Waiting at a garage, they meet a young couple who have just moved to the area and are looking for a church. A friendship begins, and a year later the couple come to faith. No one would call the breakdown a miracle. But the family never forgets whose hand was in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham said, "God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son." So they went both of them together. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Abraham was climbing a mountain to obey the hardest command God ever gave him. His son asked an innocent question, and Abraham's answer was an act of faith: God will provide. He did not know how. He only knew who. And God did provide, a ram caught in a thicket, and centuries later, on a mountain in the same region, the true Lamb who takes away the sin of the world. Providence is not only God's care for our needs. It is God providing what we need most: a Savior.

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the LORD, you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them; and you preserve all of them; and the host of heaven worships you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The returned exiles, confessing their sins, begin their prayer with God's work as Creator and Preserver: you preserve all of them. Every star, every sea creature and every human being exists at this moment because God is sustaining it. That is a humbling truth, and a steadying one. We do not hold our own lives together. He does. And the response in the same verse is worship: the host of heaven worships you.

verseByVerse.quote: that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us, for "'In him we live and move and have our being'; as even some of your own poets have said, "'For we are indeed his offspring.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Speaking to Athenian philosophers, Paul quotes their own poets: In him we live and move and have our being. Every breath, every movement and every moment of existence depends on God. Paul uses this to show that God is not far away, waiting to be discovered by clever people. He is near to everyone, sustaining them even while they ignore him. Providence is a constant witness to God's presence, and a call to seek him.

verseByVerse.quote: But a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the scale armor and the breastplate. Therefore he said to the driver of his chariot, "Turn around and carry me out of the battle, for I am wounded." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse is one of the clearest pictures of providence in Scripture. Ahab had been warned by the prophet Micaiah that he would die in battle. He tried to outwit God by disguising himself. Then an archer drew his bow at random. The arrow found the small gap in the king's armour. What looked like chance was God's word being fulfilled. No plan, however clever, can evade God's purposes.

1.reflection:
How would you explain preservation, concurrence and government in your own words?

Why is it important that God usually works through ordinary means? How should that affect the way you use medicine, work or planning?

Read 1 Kings 22. What does Ahab's death teach about providence and human schemes?

What "ordinary" event in your life do you now see as God's providence?

2.title: Providence in the Natural World
2.overview:
The Bible does not describe nature as a closed system running on its own laws. It describes it as God's world, constantly cared for by God's hand. Psalm 104 is a hymn to providence. God makes springs gush in the valleys, gives drink to the animals, causes grass to grow for livestock and plants for people, and wine to gladden the heart of man, oil to make his face shine and bread to strengthen man's heart (Ps 104:15). These all look to you, to give them their food in due season (Ps 104:27).

Weather is under God's command. He covers the heavens with clouds; he prepares rain for the earth; he makes grass grow on the hills (Ps 147:8). He gives snow like wool; he scatters frost like ashes (Ps 147:16). Elihu said that the clouds turn around and around by his guidance, to accomplish all that he commands them (Job 37:12). God sends weather for correction or for his land or for love (Job 37:13).

After the flood God promised a stable world: While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease (Gen 8:22). The regularity of nature, which science studies, is itself a gift of God's faithful providence. Scientists can study the patterns of nature because God keeps them steady.

And God's care in nature is a lesson for us. Jesus told his anxious disciples to look at the birds and the lilies. Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? (Matt 6:26). Every bird at a feeder and every flower in a field is a sermon on providence.
2.theology:
Common grace in nature: God's providence in nature reaches everyone. he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness (Acts 14:17). Paul calls this God's witness to all people. Every harvest says that there is a good Creator.

Science and providence: Scientific explanation and providence are not rivals. Meteorologists can explain how rain forms. Scripture tells us who sends it and why. Both are true at their own level. The laws of nature describe the regular way God governs his world.

Disaster and providence: Storms, earthquakes and droughts are also under God's hand. This is hard, but it is also hopeful. Natural disasters are not random cruelty; they are part of a fallen world under God's control, and they call all people to repentance (Luke 13:4-5). They also remind us that creation itself waits for redemption (Rom 8:20-22).

Gratitude: Every meal is a gift of providence. Christians give thanks before eating not out of habit, but because they know where food comes from. You open your hand; you satisfy the desire of every living thing (Ps 145:16).
2.examples:
Then: Jesus calmed a storm with a word, and the disciples asked, Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? (Mark 4:41). The one who governs the weather was in the boat with them.

Now: A farmer plants his crops, works hard and watches the sky. When rain comes at the right time, he thanks God. When drought comes, he still trusts God, prays and does what he can. He knows that he plants and waters, but God gives the growth (1 Cor 3:6).

Now: A city dweller rarely notices the weather except as an inconvenience. Reading Psalm 104, she begins to see her morning coffee, the rain on the window and the trees in the park as gifts. Her gratitude grows, and so does her trust.

Now: After a hurricane devastates a region, some say it proves God does not exist or does not care. Christians respond by grieving with the suffering, giving generously and helping rebuild, while trusting that God rules even in disaster and will one day make all things new.

verseByVerse.quote: These all look to you, to give them their food in due season. When you give it to them, they gather it up; when you open your hand, they are filled with good things. When you hide your face, they are dismayed; when you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your Spirit, they are created, and you renew the face of the ground. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Every creature looks to God for food. When God opens his hand, they are filled. When he hides his face, they are dismayed. When he takes away their breath, they die. When he sends his Spirit, new life appears. This is a picture of total dependence. Every living thing, from the smallest insect to the largest whale, depends on God moment by moment. Human beings are no exception. Our food, breath and life are gifts of his open hand.

verseByVerse.quote: Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' argument is from the lesser to the greater. If God feeds birds, which do not plant or store food, will he not care for his children? If he clothes wildflowers more beautifully than Solomon, will he not clothe you? And then the gentle rebuke: O you of little faith. Anxiety about daily needs is, at root, a failure to believe in providence. The cure is not to stop working, since birds still search for food, but to stop worrying, because the Father knows.

verseByVerse.quote: While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: After the flood, God made a covenant with all creation. The seasons would continue, the harvest would come, day would follow night. This promise is the foundation of ordinary life: farming, planning, work and rest. Every sunrise is God keeping his word to Noah. It also reminds us that the stability of the world is not guaranteed by nature itself but by God's faithfulness. While the earth remains: until the day God makes a new heaven and a new earth.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul and Barnabas had just been mistaken for gods at Lystra. Paul pointed the crowd to the true God, who did not leave himself without witness. And the witness he named was ordinary providence: rain, fruitful seasons, food and gladness. Every good harvest and every happy meal is God's testimony to his goodness. That is why ingratitude is so serious (Rom 1:21). The evidence is everywhere.

2.reflection:
Read Psalm 104 slowly. Which picture of God's care in nature moves you most?

How do scientific explanations and God's providence fit together?

Read Matthew 6:25-34. What are you most anxious about, and what does Jesus say to it?

How could you cultivate gratitude for ordinary providences, like food, weather and health, this week?

3.title: The Hidden Hand in Ordinary Lives
3.overview:
Some of the Bible's clearest lessons in providence come not through miracles but through stories in which God seems absent, and yet is everywhere.

Joseph. Joseph was hated by his brothers, thrown into a pit and sold to traders who took Joseph to Egypt (Gen 37:28). He was falsely accused and imprisoned. At every low point the narrator inserts one line: The LORD was with Joseph (Gen 39:2, 21). God was not preventing every evil, but he was present in it and working through it. Thirteen years later Joseph stood before Pharaoh, and through him God saved Egypt, the surrounding nations and his own family.

Ruth. Naomi lost her husband and both sons in a foreign land and came home bitter: the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me (Ruth 1:20). But her Moabite daughter-in-law happened to glean in Boaz's field, Boaz turned out to be a family redeemer, and the story ends with Naomi holding a grandson. They named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David (Ruth 4:17). Naomi's empty years were part of the line that led to King David, and to Christ.

Esther. God is never named in Esther. Yet the whole book turns on "coincidences." Esther becomes queen. Mordecai happens to overhear a plot against the king. And on the very night before Haman planned to ask for Mordecai's death, the king could not sleep (Esth 6:1). He asked for the royal records to be read, and they happened to include Mordecai's good deed. By morning, Haman was leading Mordecai through the city in honour.

These stories teach us to see our own lives differently. God is often most at work when we see him least.
3.theology:
God's presence is not always felt: Joseph in prison and Naomi in her grief did not feel God's care. But the narrator tells us it was there. Our feelings are not the measure of God's presence.

Providence works over time: Joseph waited about thirteen years from the pit to the palace (Gen 37:2; 41:46). Naomi's story ended with a grandson whose great-grandson would be king. Some providences are understood only after many years, and some only in eternity.

Providence includes small things: A sleepless night, a chance encounter, a forgotten good deed remembered at the right moment. Nothing is too small to be part of God's plan.

Providence points to Christ: Ruth's story ends with David's family line. Joseph's story preserves the family through whom the Messiah would come. Esther's story preserves the Jewish people. The hidden hand of providence was always guarding the line of promise that led to Jesus.
3.examples:
Then: Joseph spent years in a dungeon. A royal cupbearer promised to remember him and then forgot him for two full years (Gen 40:23; 41:1). That forgetting looked like cruel neglect. But it meant Joseph was still available at exactly the moment Pharaoh needed a dream interpreted. God's delays are not denials.

Now: A woman widowed young moves back to her hometown, discouraged and lonely. She takes a part-time job she does not want. Through that job she meets a family who need help caring for an elderly parent, and through them she finds a church, deep friendships and, years later, a ministry to other widows. Looking back, she says, "I called myself Mara, like Naomi. God had other plans."

Now: A Christian student's application to a prestigious university is rejected. He attends a smaller college instead, where he joins a campus ministry that shapes his whole life. He later says that rejection was one of God's kindest gifts.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man, and he was in the house of his Egyptian master. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This short sentence is the key to Joseph's story. He was a slave in a foreign land, cut off from his father and betrayed by his brothers. Yet The LORD was with Joseph. It is repeated in the prison (Gen 39:21). God's presence did not mean the absence of suffering. It meant that suffering was never the whole story. The same promise is given to every believer: I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matt 28:20).

verseByVerse.quote: She said to them, "Do not call me Naomi; call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. I went away full, and the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi, when the LORD has testified against me and the Almighty has brought calamity upon me?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Naomi's grief is honest. She does not deny God's sovereignty; she blames it. the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. She went away full and came back empty. Scripture does not rebuke her. It lets her speak, and then it shows her story unfolding. Within weeks a kinsman-redeemer would appear, and by the end of the book she would be holding a child in her lap. Naomi saw only the bitterness. God saw the whole story.

verseByVerse.quote: So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And he went in to her, and the LORD gave her conception, and she bore a son. Then the women said to Naomi, "Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer, and may his name be renowned in Israel! He shall be to you a restorer of life and a nourisher of your old age, for your daughter-in-law who loves you, who is more to you than seven sons, has given birth to him." Then Naomi took the child and laid him on her lap and became his nurse. And the women of the neighborhood gave him a name, saying, "A son has been born to Naomi." They named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The book that began with three funerals ends with a birth. The women of Bethlehem praise God: Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a redeemer. The bitter widow becomes a grandmother. And the last verse reaches far beyond Naomi: Obed was the father of Jesse, the father of David. Naomi could never have imagined that her sorrows were part of the story that would lead to Israel's greatest king, and to the Son of David himself.

verseByVerse.quote: On that night the king could not sleep. And he gave orders to bring the book of memorable deeds, the chronicles, and they were read before the king. And it was found written how Mordecai had told about Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, who guarded the threshold, and who had sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus. And the king said, "What honor or distinction has been bestowed on Mordecai for this?" The king's young men who attended him said, "Nothing has been done for him." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: On that night the king could not sleep. Of all the nights in Persian history, this was the one that mattered. A sleepless king, a servant reading the royal records, a page about Mordecai's good deed, and a question: What honor or distinction has been bestowed on Mordecai for this? The answer: nothing. Everything was set up for Haman's downfall and Mordecai's honour, through a king's insomnia. God does not need to be named to be at work.

3.reflection:
Read the book of Esther (it takes less than an hour). Make a list of the "coincidences." What do they reveal?

Like Naomi, have you ever felt that God has dealt bitterly with you? How does the end of Ruth speak to that?

Why do you think God sometimes works most when he seems most absent?

What delay or disappointment in your life might be part of God's hidden providence?

4.title: Hard Providences
4.overview:
Not all providences are pleasant. Scripture speaks honestly of providences that wound: loss, sickness, disappointment, grief and pain. Job lost his children, his wealth and his health. His wife told him to curse God and die. He answered, Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil? (Job 2:10). Job was not saying that God does evil. He was acknowledging that the hard things in his life had come under God's hand, and he refused to turn against God.

Paul knew hard providences too. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself (2 Cor 1:8). But he saw a purpose in it: that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead (2 Cor 1:9).

Scripture gives several reasons why God sends hard providences to his children. They discipline us in love: For the Lord disciplines the one he loves (Heb 12:6). They turn us back: Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word (Ps 119:67). They refine our faith like gold in a fire (1 Pet 1:6-7; Job 23:10). They teach dependence (2 Cor 1:9). They display God's works (John 9:3). And they prepare glory: For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison (2 Cor 4:17).

But Scripture also guards us against cruel conclusions. Hard providences are not always punishment for a particular sin. When the disciples asked whether a man was born blind because of his sin or his parents', Jesus said, It was not that this man sinned, or his parents, but that the works of God might be displayed in him (John 9:3). And God does not delight in our pain: for he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men (Lam 3:33).
4.theology:
Do not read providence as a verdict: We cannot look at someone's suffering and conclude that God is punishing them. Job's friends made that mistake, and God rebuked them (Job 42:7). Jesus warned that those killed when a tower fell were not worse sinners than others (Luke 13:4-5). Every disaster is a call for all of us to repent, not a verdict on its victims.

God's heart in affliction: Lamentations 3:32-33 holds two truths: God may cause grief, and yet he does not afflict from his heart. He is sovereign over suffering, but he takes no pleasure in it for its own sake. His compassion is according to the abundance of his steadfast love.

Christ in our suffering: Christians do not face hard providences alone. Christ suffered, and he is with us. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you (Isa 43:2). He does not always take us around the waters, but he always goes through them with us.

Good for me: Many believers can say with the psalmist, It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes (Ps 119:71). Not good in itself, but good in what God did with it.
4.examples:
Then: God led Israel through the wilderness for forty years. Moses later explained, he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna ... that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone (Deut 8:3). The hunger was providence. So was the manna. Both taught Israel to depend on God.

Now: A young couple long for children and face years of infertility. Well-meaning friends offer explanations. The couple learn instead to bring their grief honestly to God, as Hannah did (1 Sam 1). They do not know how God will answer. But they find that hard providence has drawn them closer to each other and to him.

Now: A pastor diagnosed with a long illness has to step back from ministry. He grieves. Over time he discovers that his weakness gives him a new tenderness toward the sick and suffering, and the letters he writes from his bed comfort more people than his sermons ever did. He can say with Paul that what happened to him has really served to advance the gospel (Phil 1:12).

Now: A believer whose friend's child has died resists every temptation to explain. He brings meals, sits with them, prays and waits. Hard providences call for presence more than explanations.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to her, "You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Job had lost everything, and now he was covered in sores. His wife's advice was despair: curse God and die. Job's answer is one of the great statements of faith in Scripture: Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil? He did not pretend his suffering was good, and he would later pour out his anguish honestly. But he refused to believe that God was good only when life was pleasant. In all this Job did not sin with his lips.

verseByVerse.quote: For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself. Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead. He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul does not hide his weakness. He was utterly burdened beyond our strength, so much that he expected to die. But he saw God's purpose: to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead. Hard providences strip away our self-reliance. And Paul's response is hope in three tenses: God delivered us, he will deliver us, and he will deliver us again. The God who raises the dead can be trusted with every situation that feels like death.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lord will not cast off forever, for, though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love; for he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jeremiah writes from the ruins of Jerusalem, and in the middle of his grief he finds solid ground. God will not cast off forever. Even when he causes grief, he will have compassion. And he does not afflict from his heart. God is not cruel. Affliction is not what he most delights in. It is a tool in the hands of a compassionate Father, used for a time and for a purpose, and always within the bounds of his steadfast love.

verseByVerse.quote: And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? "My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives." It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons. Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The writer calls hard providences discipline, and discipline is a sign of sonship. God is treating you as sons. A father who never corrected his child would not be a loving father. And the writer is honest: For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant. But it has a harvest: the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it. Hard providences are not signs that God has abandoned us. They are signs that he is raising us as his children.

4.reflection:
What hard providence have you experienced? How did it affect your faith at the time, and how do you see it now?

Why is it wrong to conclude that someone is suffering because of a particular sin? How should we respond instead?

Read Psalm 119:65-72. Can you say, "It is good for me that I was afflicted"? Why or why not?

How can you be present with someone going through a hard providence this week?

5.title: Providence, Guidance and Our Choices
5.overview:
If God governs all things, how should we make decisions? Christians often ask how to know God's will about a job, a marriage, a move or a ministry. Scripture's teaching on providence gives a clear and freeing answer.

God guides through his word. His revealed will in Scripture tells us how to live: what to believe, what to do and what to avoid. Most of God's will for us is already written. The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us (Deut 29:29). If a choice would break God's commands, we do not need any further guidance.

God guides through wisdom. Within the boundaries of Scripture, God usually expects us to make wise choices using prayer, good sense and counsel. Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths (Prov 3:5-6). God promises to guide those who trust him, but he does not usually tell us his plan in advance.

God guides through providence. God opens and closes doors through circumstances. Paul wanted to visit Rome for years but wrote that he had so often been hindered (Rom 15:22). He accepted that, prayed and kept working. Circumstances are part of how God directs our steps.

But here a caution is needed. Providence is not a new word from God. Circumstances can be read in many ways, and an open door is not always God's will (Jonah found a ship going to Tarshish). In the book of Acts the apostles sometimes received direct revelation (Acts 16:6-10), but that was part of the foundational apostolic ministry. Believers today should not expect visions or inner voices to settle their decisions. We have Scripture, which is sufficient (2 Tim 3:16-17), the gift of wisdom and the counsel of God's people. And we can make decisions in freedom, trusting that God will direct our steps even through our imperfect choices: The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps (Prov 16:9).
5.theology:
God's will of command and decree: God's revealed will (his commands) is what we must obey. His decretive will (his plan) is what he will bring about. We are responsible for the first. We do not need to discover the second before acting; we trust it.

No need for anxiety: Many Christians are paralysed by fear of missing "God's perfect will" in decisions like which job or house to choose. Scripture does not teach that there is a single right choice hidden in every decision that we must discover. Where God has not commanded, we choose wisely and freely, and his providence holds us.

Circumstances need interpretation: A closed door may mean "not this way," or it may be a test of perseverance. An open door may be an opportunity, or a temptation. That is why circumstances must always be weighed by Scripture and wise counsel, not treated as signs.

Using means: Trusting providence does not make planning, effort, medicine or prudence unnecessary. God provides through these means. Nehemiah prayed and posted guards (Neh 4:9). Faith and prudence work together.
5.examples:
Then: Jonah wanted to run from God, and providence seemed to cooperate: he went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish (Jonah 1:3). An open door. But it was the wrong direction, and God sent a storm. Convenient circumstances are not the same as God's approval.

Now: A young man is choosing between two jobs. Both are honest work. He prays, asks the advice of older believers, considers which job would allow him to serve his family and church better, and makes a decision. He does not wait for a sign. He trusts that God will direct his steps, and moves forward in freedom.

Now: A woman feels strongly that God is "telling her" to leave her husband, though there is no biblical ground for it. Her pastor gently points out that God does not lead against his written word. Feelings and impressions must always be tested by Scripture.

Now: A church considering a building project has a large gift fall through. Rather than seeing it as a definitive "no" from God, the leaders pray, seek counsel and consider whether the timing or the plan needs adjusting. They read providence carefully and humbly.

verseByVerse.quote: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: These verses are often quoted in times of decision, and rightly. But notice what they actually promise. They do not promise that God will reveal his plan in advance. They promise that if we trust him with all our heart and acknowledge him in all our ways, he will make straight your paths. The emphasis is on our trust and God's guidance, not on our knowledge of the future. We walk by faith, and God makes the path straight, often in ways we see only looking back.

verseByVerse.quote: The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This proverb frees us from two errors. We are to plan; the heart of man plans his way. Planning is not unspiritual. But God establishes our steps. Our plans are not the final word. We can therefore plan diligently and hold our plans loosely, knowing that God may redirect us, and that his redirection will be good. Many believers' best experiences of providence were plans that God changed.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul had longed to visit Rome for years. He prayed about it constantly (Rom 1:10). Yet he had so often been hindered. He did not conclude that God did not want him to go. Nor did he force his way. He kept praying, kept working and kept planning. In the end, he did reach Rome, as a prisoner, by a route he never would have chosen (Acts 28). Providence often fulfils our desires in ways we do not expect.

verseByVerse.quote: I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go; I will counsel you with my eye upon you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God promises, I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go; I will counsel you with my eye upon you. The image is of a teacher watching over a student. God does not leave his people to wander alone. He guides through his word and watches over us in his providence. The next verse warns against being like a mule that must be controlled by bit and bridle (Ps 32:9). God wants willing children who walk with him, not stubborn animals who must be dragged.

5.reflection:
How have you usually tried to discern God's will in decisions? How does this unit confirm or challenge your approach?

Why is it dangerous to treat circumstances or inner impressions as new words from God?

What decision are you facing? How could you apply Scripture, prayer, wisdom and counsel to it?

How does Proverbs 16:9 free you from anxiety about making the "wrong" choice?

6.title: Living by Providence
6.overview:
The doctrine of providence is meant to change the way we live day by day. It produces several distinct graces in a believer's life.

Contentment. Paul wrote from prison, for I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content (Phil 4:11). He had known plenty and hunger, abundance and need, and in every case he found strength in Christ. Contentment is not passive resignation. It is trust that God's providence has placed us where we are for good reasons. be content with what you have, for he has said, "I will never leave you nor forsake you." (Heb 13:5).

Gratitude. give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you (1 Thess 5:18). Not for all circumstances, as if evil were good, but in them, because God is at work in all of them.

Courage. When Elisha's servant saw an enemy army surrounding the city, he was terrified. Elisha said, Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them, and prayed that the servant's eyes would be opened. and he saw, and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha (2 Kgs 6:16-17). Providence means we are never as alone or unprotected as we feel.

Patience. Providence often moves slowly. Joseph waited years, Abraham waited decades. Trusting providence means waiting for God's timing.

Remembrance. After a great victory Samuel set up a stone and called it Ebenezer, for he said, "Till now the LORD has helped us." (1 Sam 7:12). Believers grow in trust by looking back. I will remember the deeds of the LORD (Ps 77:11).

Rest. He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber (Ps 121:3). We can sleep at night, because God does not.
6.theology:
Providence and prayer: Providence does not make prayer pointless. God has ordained to work through the prayers of his people. We pray because God is sovereign, not in spite of it.

Providence and contentment: Discontent is, at root, a complaint against God's providence. It says, "God has not given me what I need." Contentment says, The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want (Ps 23:1).

Providence and assurance: Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever (Ps 23:6). The providence that guides us now will bring us safely home.

Providence and worship: Jacob, returning home after twenty years, prayed, I am not worthy of the least of all the deeds of steadfast love and all the faithfulness that you have shown to your servant (Gen 32:10). The more we see God's providence, the more we worship.
6.examples:
Then: Jacob left home with nothing but a staff. God promised, Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go (Gen 28:15). Twenty years later Jacob returned with a large family and great wealth. He looked back and said that he had crossed the Jordan with only a staff, and now had become two camps (Gen 32:10). Providence had kept every promise.

Now: A family keeps a "providence journal." Each week they write down one way they saw God's care: a provision, a protection, an answered prayer, a kindness from a stranger. After a few years they read it back together and are amazed. It has become their family's Ebenezer stone.

Now: An elderly Christian is asked how she stayed faithful through war, loss, illness and widowhood. She answers, "I learned that I did not have to understand God's providence to trust it. He never failed me once."

This week: Begin a providence journal. Read Psalm 121 each night before sleep. Thank God for one ordinary provision each day. And when something goes wrong, say, "The LORD will provide," and look for his hand.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that I am speaking of being in need, for I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content. I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. In any and every circumstance, I have learned the secret of facing plenty and hunger, abundance and need. I can do all things through him who strengthens me. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul did not say contentment came naturally. He said I have learned it. He learned it through experience of both plenty and need. And the secret is in verse 13: I can do all things through him who strengthens me. That famous verse is not a promise that we can achieve anything we want. It is a promise that in every circumstance God places us, Christ will give us strength to be content. Providence and contentment belong together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen and called its name Ebenezer; for he said, "Till now the LORD has helped us." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Samuel set up a stone as a memorial of God's help. The name means "stone of help," and the meaning is given in the verse: Till now the LORD has helped us. Every believer needs Ebenezer stones, reminders of past providences that give confidence for the future. "Till now" looks back with gratitude. It also looks forward with hope: the God who has helped us thus far will not abandon us now.

verseByVerse.quote: He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This psalm was probably sung by pilgrims travelling to Jerusalem, facing dangers on the road. The repeated word is keep. God keeps your foot, keeps your life, keeps your going out and coming in. And he will neither slumber nor sleep. Human guardians grow tired; God never does. Every night when we sleep, the God of providence is awake, watching over us. That is why believers can rest.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name's sake. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me. You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows. Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The best-loved psalm is a psalm of providence. The shepherd provides (green pastures, still waters), restores, leads, protects (the valley of the shadow of death), comforts, feeds and pursues. Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life. The word "follow" suggests pursuit. God's goodness does not merely accompany us. It chases us down every road. And the journey ends at home: I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever.

6.reflection:
Read Philippians 4:10-13. In which situation do you most need to learn contentment?

What "Ebenezer stones" can you identify in your own life, times when "till now the LORD has helped us"?

How does Psalm 121 change the way you think about your safety and your sleep?

Start a providence journal this week. What is the first entry?
